utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning. Today we are sitting in a new hall where there are some slight changes, but I hope that after a while, we shall get used to them. Today we have before us -- the registrar, will you please tell us the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IT-95-14/1-T, the Tribunal against Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Will you please tell us who is presenting the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, my name is Niemann, and I appear with my colleague, Mr. Meddegoda, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. Mr. Mikulicic, will you tell us who is here for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My name is Goran Mikulicic, and with my colleague, Joka, I am representing the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Mikulicic, it is now your turn to begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we should like to call the witness, Anto Jerkovic, who has already been brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Anto Jerkovic. Can you hear me? I am speaking to you. Can you hear me? You will now read the solemn declaration which you have here before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may sit down, sir, and answer the questions which Mr. Mikulicic will be asking you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in view of the new circumstances or, rather, new environment in this courtroom, permit me to address the witness from this place because I have this documentation which is here, at my bench, or am I supposed to go out and speak from that microphone as it has been envisaged here? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I believe that you can speak from your place. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have just received a message from my Defendant that he is not feeling well, that he has some health problems, and he is kindly asking you if we could make a brief recess to see what is wrong. Well, you can, of course, see what the problem is, and whether we can then continue? If I may, Your Honour, I should like to talk to my client to see what is wrong with him. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Aleksovski is not feeling well because, on his way to the court, he has been put in a room which is very small and where there is not air, and this environment, the ambient atmosphere has affected his health. He says he feels quite all right, but he needs a little bit more air. So could he please be kept in some other room? In this particular room, there is simply some bad smell, and it affects him. So that is his basic problem. He believes that it could be solved by simply taking a very short break and taking him to a room which is likely more airy and which is less contaminated by some bad smell. I don't know what it's all about. I don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, is there a way in which we could meet this request?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No. At the moment, I'm afraid I cannot answer this question. During the break, I could perhaps see -- the deputy registrar see if we can move to another room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mikulicic, could we continue now, or does Mr. Aleksovski need a break or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksovski says that he will manage until the first break, and then we shall see what we can do about moving him to another room, so we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Right. So we shall then proceed. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jerkovic.

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My name is Goran Mikulicic, I am here for the Defence, and I shall ask you some questions, and I will ask you now some questions, and please answer them to the best of your recollection. Mr. Jerkovic, will you tell us where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, 1954, in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you a believer?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What religion do you belong to?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Croat. I'm of the Croat religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, will you tell us something about your education?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I have grade -- elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where did you attend elementary school?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Stranjane. Elementary school, Luka Jelicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: There must some error in the answer to the question what his religion was. It couldn't be of the Croat religion, it must be something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. We shall correct that in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, I asked you what religion did you belong to. Were you Catholic or Orthodox?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Roman Catholic, you mean. Sir, you said you have elementary school. Where did you live during your education?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Janjal near Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was your first job and where; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not remember the first time, but I worked for a Sarajevo company at the Zenica steel works. The acronym was BRALIM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, is it true that you got a job with the penitentiary in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: 4th of April, 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What were you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I was a guard, security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Therefore, as of 1978, you have been with the penitentiary in Zenica as a security guard. Until when were you there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I worked there until -- I do not know exactly, but until 1992, until I was mobilised as a military policeman for the B and H army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In other words, while you were the guard of the penitentiary, a war broke out in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then the army of B and H mobilised you to the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that mobilisation, did you continue keeping your job at the penitentiary or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I worked at the penitentiary, but there was a department which was part of the military police but it was within the penitentiary complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. If I'm correct, you said it was sometime in the latter half of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, while you were employed with the penitentiary in Zenica, did you perhaps meet Mr. Aleksovski there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when you met him for the first time? When was that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what post -- what was Mr. Aleksovski at the penitentiary in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was an educator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you recognise Mr. Aleksovski if you saw him today?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you recognise him now, whether he's in his room?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the gentleman up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has indicated in the direction of the accused, Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, you said, therefore, that Mr. Aleksovski was an educator at the Zenica penitentiary?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what was his -- how did he treat the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was good, it was great.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you then tell us -- of course, if you know -- what was his duty as an educator at the penitentiary? What did he do?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he took care of the prisoners. I mean, he took care of everything, about the state of their health, about their leaves, weekends, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Can you remember if, at that time, there were any problems between Mr. Aleksovski and the inmates? Did they complain against him or not; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't recall that there were ever any problems. Everything was, by and large, quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, do you remember if, at that time, Mr. Aleksovski treated the prisoners differently because of their religion, I mean Muslims or Croats? Did he distinguish between them or did he treat them all equally?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, at a later stage, towards the end of 1992, you volunteered for the HVO; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us to what HVO unit were you assigned when you volunteered?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: The military police again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The military police.

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So where were you deployed? Where were you when you became a member of the HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I was deployed in Vitez, in Vitez, and then when I came for the job, I was told that I would go to Kaonik, to the prison in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was, roughly?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you came to the military district prison at Kaonik on the 7th of January, 1993, as a military policeman. Could you tell us, were you security?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Prison security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In other words, as a guard?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Mr. Jerkovic, while you were still with the penitentiary in Zenica, which is again a prison, isn't it --

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- do you remember under what Ministry was that penitentiary in Zenica, under whose jurisdiction was it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said on the 7th of January, 1993, you were appointed as a guard at the district military prison at Kaonik. Do you know under which Ministry was it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was that same Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, at the time when you came to Kaonik to the district military prison, who were and were there at all any prisoners at the district military prison?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when I came, there were some under disciplinary measures which the commanders -- that is, people sanctioned by the commanders. There were a couple of soldiers, I remember, perhaps one or two soldiers, one or two persons against whom criminal proceedings were being conducted by the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember which military court? From where?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: From Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if the district military court in Travnik also had some detainees at the Kaonik district prison?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: The district military court in Travnik with a seat in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So at the time when you came to Kaonik, you found there some detainees detained there on two different grounds. Some had been remanded into custody by the district military court, and others were there serving disciplinary punishment pronounced on some HVO soldiers by their commanders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were there some other persons at the district military prison in Kaonik or only those that you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Only those that we have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, do you remember how many guards were employed by the district military prison in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know the exact number. I can give you a rough figure because I do not remember exactly. About 15 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And how were they organised? Did they take shifts or how?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they took shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many shifts were there, one, two, three, four? How many shifts?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: We worked 12, 24. Those were our working hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean 12 hours on duty and then 24 hours off and then again and so on?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. How many guards were on a shift?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: On a shift, there were four, five people. Five.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were all these guards members of the military police or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were they all?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, do you remember the outbreak of the conflict between Muslims and Croats in the area of Busovaca in January 1993? Do you remember when it began?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, on the 24th, 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you, perhaps, remember the event which triggered this conflict, the event?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: It began with the murder of Ivica Petrovic on the road to the village of Dusina. It was that. I think it was that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you then tell us who was Ivica Petrovic who was killed in the village of Kacuni? Was he a Croat, a Serb, a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: A Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, that village of Kacuni where the incident happened, the population who lived in that village, was it a Muslim village or a Croat or was it mixed; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not from Zenica, so I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you don't know?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that this incident marked the beginning of the conflict on the 25th of January, 1993 between Muslims and Croats in the area of the municipality of Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that event, did the conflict escalate? I mean, the armed fighting? Was there any fire; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I was commuting. I was commuting from home to work and back. As there were no problems and nothing, so I commuted from work to home and from home to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time, you lived in Zenica still?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As long as the roads were open, you travelled normally from Zenica to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How far is it? Do you remember how many kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe around 20, 25 kilometres, 22, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, after the 25th when armed fighting began, you could not travel any more; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Then you had to stay in Kaonik. You couldn't go back to Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time, did you stay within Kaonik? Did you sleep there or live there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, could you tell us, after the conflict broke out in the area of the municipality of Busovaca, do you remember if any civilians were brought to Kaonik from the territory of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how? Were they transported to Kaonik? Were they brought by the HVO army or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: By the military police, the army of HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did the HVO policemen say when they brought them to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: That they had to be accommodated and that they had to stay there until it calmed down, until things became clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So is that true, that the military police brought those people to accommodate them temporarily until the conflict ended; is that what you were told?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you present at the time when those people were brought to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, the Kaonik facility, it was the barracks of the former JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that facility comprises several buildings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was the purpose of those buildings in the JNA time?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Those were hangars, ammunition depot, I mean, explosive devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And one of those hangars which housed the district military prison was rebuilt, redone into cells; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many cells were there in one of the buildings which was redone in that manner?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: About 14 or 15, I don't remember exactly, but about 14 or 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, can you tell us, in these cells, were there already some detainees, as you told us a moment ago? How many more people could be accommodated there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, one could put there -- well, about 50 to 60 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Jerkovic, how many people did the military police bring out of the conflict in the territory of Busovaca to Kaonik? How many of them? Was it more than 50 or 60 or less?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: More.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Jerkovic, that you could not accommodate these people in the prison facilities?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So where did you put these people if you could not put them in the prison facility?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: There is a hangar next to this hangar, and then we put them there, because down there they could not fit in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, you said that you came to Kaonik on the 7th of January, '93?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Has anyone from that day -- did anyone between that day, the day when you were informed that civilians would be brought in, did anybody there tell you that this would happen?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you could not prepare any accommodation facilities for those people?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But you nevertheless managed somehow; you provided some accommodation. Could you tell us, what did you do in order to provide them with some accommodation facilities?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we had some racks, some shelves that were there. I don't know what they were for, and we put them down there. And we took also some boards, some wooden planks, to put them down, and some blankets. So some they put underneath and some they used to cover themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, the people that were brought by the military police in Kaonik, did you, in any way, make any lists about them?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: It was already dusk, and there was a table, and all approached that table, and we put their names on a list. And I know from previous experience in Zenica how this protocol is made, so whether I was there or somebody else -- and since I had the most experience and the others hadn't such an experience because they didn't work in penitentiaries before, individually, we invited each of them to approach the table and put their names, family names and first names. And then we took some documents -- not documents, but if they had something on them, knives and other things, for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you said that when these people were approached that you made a list that identified themselves and that you took away from them some objects that could be, you know, arms, like knives; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me again, did you take some private things from them like private possessions like money, like watches, like jewellery, or did you leave that on them?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't take that because we didn't have anywhere to put it. And it remained with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that when they were brought, it was already dark and that for the reception and a listing, that it was done in a hangar that was above the prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there any electricity in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How could you see then? How could you write their names and surnames? Did you have --

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we brought the candle. Because there were frequent electricity cuts, we had candles, and I brought one or two candles. And that's how we wrote their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Jerkovic, that there were frequent electricity cuts. Does that mean that the situation was such that the entire facility of Kaonik would remain without electricity?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what was the situation with water supply? Were there any cuts again?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: That situation was poor too as far as water supply is concerned. It was cold. The pipes broke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, however, in the vicinity of that hangar, there was a well, is that correct, from where you could take water when there was no water in the facility, when the pipes broke down? Do you remember, was there a well or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: The well, it was not so close, yes, but we did bring some water. It was further down there, but we had some plastic containers later from which we took water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So there were problems with water supply?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, tell us, the people who were placed in that hangar, how did you organise -- what was the organisation in the hangar when people had to go to the toilet, when they had to wash themselves, to take a bath?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we did make some makeshift toilet outside. So the guard who was there, the prisoner would knock and they would let him out. And as for washing, we had some -- we took from the army large containers, and we brought water, and it was taken in and then they could wash up their faces and...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, so you were there with those people, with people who were taken from Busovaca. Did you personally notice or see that these people were beaten or harassed or maltreated in any other way. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you find yourself in a situation that some of these people would complain to you because of the treatment of some guards or something like that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did some of these people complain to you about health problems or did they seek medical care?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: We took them to the outpatient units in Busovaca to see the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did you take them there? Did you have a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had a vehicle, but you never knew what could happen because it broke down. So doctors would frequently come to the prison in order to check up on the prisoners or for some other business.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that somebody who sought medical care or to see a doctor, that this was refused or denied?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that all those who sought medical care could receive it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you took those persons to the doctor in Busovaca, how far is it from Kaonik? How many kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, about five kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were they handcuffed or were their hands tied in any way?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you took them to see a doctor, where did they wait to see the doctor?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, where the other people were sitting, like, civilians. There was an area where people were waiting to see a doctor, and they were brought there, and they waited along with the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So there were no special protection and safety measures like being handcuffed and surveillance of these people when they were taken to see a doctor?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, do you remember when Zlatko Aleksovski came to Kaonik; before or after you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: He came after, I think, at the start of February. I can't remember exactly the date, at the end of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the people that were brought by military police from Busovaca, and these civilians, how long did they say in Kaonik, until which date?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly the date, but it was for a short time, a very short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. What was the food? What did these people eat and where was the food brought to them, from where?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: We had all the same food. Some food was brought from Draga. We had a kitchen down there, and people would bring food, the same food for us and for prisoners. It was the same food. There was no difference. We all ate from the same mess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said now that some part of the food was brought from Draga. Is that Draga, was that a barrack, an HVO barracks or what?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: It was an HVO barrack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was it in the area of Busovaca or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: In the area of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You also said that food was prepared in a kitchen that was part of the same facility in Kaonik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where was the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: At the very entrance of the Kaonik barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who was in that building? Who was accommodated there in that facility which served as a kitchen?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, we had a cook who was preparing food for us in the military police at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there also military policemen, not guards, but members of the military police units?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were some of them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it then correct that the cook who prepared food in that facility was cooking for members of the military police who were accommodated in that facility and for prisoners and detainees, civilians who were in the district prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Jerkovic, what were the meals? What kind of food did you eat?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, we had beans, potatoes, you know, things like that, lentils.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there any meat?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many meals a day were prepared in this way?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Three, three meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, in the room in which people were temporarily accommodated, in that hangar, was there any heating there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had a furnace there, because there were two in the prison, and then one was put up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you took the furnace up there when the people were brought there in order to warm them up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether these people were preparing tea on that furnace?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were large utensils in which they could prepare tea, and people were drinking tea all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This furnace, what kind of fuel was used, timber, oil?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly timber, wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who was feeding the furnace?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: They themselves did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where did they find wood? Was there enough wood?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not really, because we were cutting wood around the prison because it is in the woods. So we could cut wood there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, so there was not enough wood that was prepared for heating, so you had to cut wood in the surrounding woods; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Jerkovic, we were discussing and we heard that people could see a doctor if they sought so in Busovaca. Do you remember that after seeing some of these people, the doctor would seek, for instance, a release on medical grounds; do you remember that? Were there any cases like that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you accept those medical instructions? Did you release those people and send them home?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did accept the instructions from the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You also said that those people were temporarily placed in that facility. And during that time, did they have some compulsory obligations like work; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that these civilians were taken from Kaonik for compulsory work outside the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who would come to take them out from Kaonik for compulsory work obligations?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: The army, HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When the army came there and asked to be given a certain number of people for compulsory work obligation, what would they say? Where were they taking them?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Trench digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, how did you select people for trench digging? Was it at random or did you have some other way of who was going to do that? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: We had a list of all people. When they were brought to prison, because it was cold, all the people were put to prison cells downstairs because we were trying to put the elderly and the sick down there in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why, because conditions were better?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely because of that. And the others who were up there in the hangar, we had a list and we selected -- there was a roll call, when we needed 10 or 15 people, and we checked out or put a mark of how many people were taken, so that we know who was taken in order to avoid repetition, or all the same people would be doing that job all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is that then correct, that, in this way, you took care to distribute the burden evenly?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you also take care about medical recommendations, so when the doctor said that some people should not be taken out to work?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You also said, Mr. Jerkovic, that for trench digging and compulsory work obligation, that they were taken by military police of the HVO. Did they drive them also?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did somebody from the guards, from Kaonik, accompany them or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that when HVO army or military police took them from Kaonik, that they were responsible for those people?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, when these people were returned to you from compulsory work obligation, when they were returned to Kaonik, did you see or check that the same people were returned to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice at any time that some of the people who were returned to you, that they were injured or wounded, or did something like that happen?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was your reaction? Did you take these people to see the doctor?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you complain to the military police about the injuring of these people when they were outside Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did it sometimes happen that people who were taken away for compulsory work obligation were not returned to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What would you then do when you saw that somebody was not returned to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: We would report about that, and then we would ask them what happened, and we were told that they escaped, simply that they escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you personally know that there were such escapes from compulsory work obligation? Did you personally know that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know of a case, of an event that happened shortly before these people were released from Kaonik, were released to go home, that two of them were taken for work obligation, that they died? Do you know of such an event?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know that connected with that, that criminal proceedings were instigated before a court because of that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, you also said that after military police, HVO military police, would take people out from Kaonik for their compulsory work obligation, that they were then under their responsibility and jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you know that people who were taken out from Kaonik in this way were used as human shields?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did some of those people ever tell you that they were used as a human shield at any occasion? Have you heard something like that from anyone?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, you also said that Aleksovski came to Kaonik at the end of January or beginning of February, you can't remember the date. What was the way in which he treated prisoners and people who were detained, like civilians from Busovaca? What was his treatment?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Aleksovski met their requests in some ways, whether he would allow them to go home, to take some clothing, or whether he allowed them -- that their families brought them food? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, things like that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the people who were Muslims by religion, whether these people had the opportunity to observe their religious ceremonies?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Whether they used that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Whether somebody from the guards prevented them from observing their religious beliefs?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, do you remember that, in Kaonik, precisely for that purpose, for religious purposes, a Muslim priest or a hodja would arrive?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where did he come from, from which place; do you know that? From Busovaca or from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where from, but he did arrive there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, tell me, when this hodja would arrive, did he have the opportunity to remain alone with the believers for these religious purposes?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did somebody disturb them then?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the priest or the hodja, would he bring with him some food for his believers?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he brought some cakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We spoke about the Kaonik facility as a former JNA barracks. Do you know that -- although you are not from that area, but you did work there for some time, do you know whether, in the area of Busovaca there was any similar facility like the former JNA barracks at Kaonik where a large number of people were accommodated, or was Kaonik the only such facility in the Busovaca area?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that Kaonik was the only such facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, the people who were brought shortly after the first conflict broke out on the 25th or 26th of January remained for some time in Kaonik. You said you don't remember when they were released from Kaonik. But in any case, after the first conflict between the Croats and Muslims, there was a lull; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So occasionally the roads were secure and you could use them -- how long did it last? -- when a new armed conflict broke out in the Busovaca area?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I think in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In April. Did any of the civilians that were taken to Kaonik at the end of January, were they there in February or March, until the renewal of armed conflicts, or they were all released?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: They were all released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So in the interval between the first conflict at the end of January and the second conflict somewhere in April, is it true then that in Kaonik only detainees from the district military court were accommodated?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So no other civilians were there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So when the conflict broke out for the second time, and you already said it was in April, were again people from the area of Busovaca, the municipality of Busovaca, brought to Kaonik once again, as in the first case?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Very few. Very few, not really, but there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what villages those people came, if you know those villages, as you are not a local man?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That second conflict was quite fierce; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time, some changes happened as regards the guards at Kaonik; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in April, the guards, and you just said those are military policemen, in Kaonik, were mobilised from the prison and sent to the frontline?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In other words, sometime in April, you left Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why did you have to leave Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: There were very few people, there was a lot of problems, and on the frontline, simply very many people, even those under disciplinary measures, were released and sent to the frontline, and we also went to the frontline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Muslim attacks were so forceful that all the men capable of defence had to be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did this involve also people who were under disciplinary sanctions, rather, who were serving for disciplinary reasons, were they also mobilised?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, after the guards, after the military police left Kaonik, do you know who took over the security of Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Domobrans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, for the record, could you explain who are Domobrans, what category of people are they?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these are mostly elderly men, over 50 or 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that those people were reserve and were mobilised as such?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But who, in view of their age, were not capable of participating in combat?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So these people were then appointed as guards in Kaonik to replace the military police?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that the defence lines, when they were deployed, were actually very close to Kaonik; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how far was it from the Kaonik facility, how far was the defence line from it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for instance, those sides which were the closest, well, there was at the Lasva River, Bulva, but as the crow flies, perhaps a kilometre, kilometre and a half or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Kaonik facility, in view of that nearness from the defence lines, as the crow flies, does it mean that it was also exposed to fire?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, of your own knowledge, whether any of the detainees or internees in Kaonik were injured due to this, that is, suffer an injury because of a shell or whatever which perhaps hit Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that two or three Domobrans were injured by shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You're referring to guards, also Domobrans?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Domobrans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But were any of the prisoners injured?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, do you remember if Kaonik prison and the whole facility was ever visited by representatives of international organisations?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which were those organisations?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: The Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did the representatives of the Red Cross visiting Kaonik have an opportunity of talking to prisoners and internees? Could they talk to them?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: They could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could they talk to them, that is, without the presence of guards?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could the prisoners send letters or messages to their families through the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In that sense, that is communication through the Red Cross, did the prison guards or the prison warden ever forbid any such communication?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Since we mention now the prison warden, we shall also say something about Mr. Aleksovski. You said he arrived sometime towards the end of January or early February to become the commander of the prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski a member of the military police like the guards in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he was a member of any other military unit, if not the military police, was he a member of any military unit?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Jerkovic, we've heard in the earlier proceedings from witnesses that they saw Mr. Aleksovski in a military uniform at times. Did you ever see him wearing a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did he have any insignia, any patches or any rank insignia, on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No. At the time, everybody sported such uniforms. I mean, I saw him usually wearing a vest and also civilian trousers or something like that, or even those military -- German military jumpers or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned jumpers of the German army. Could you remind us all here in the courtroom what kind of jumpers are those? What are they?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they are sweaters, knitwear, and they have something in leather and then the flag, I think, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So it was a military sweater with a German flag on the sleeve; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Once (sic) those sweaters?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you so that the Court could hear. Could you buy them in a shop?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was it kind of aid or relief that was sent in clothing?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, you mentioned that Mr. Aleksovski wore a military uniform at times but that it was a common sight at the time, that is, civilians wore them. Why was that so? What do you think? Could the reason be that the supply in clothing and footwear was poor?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. There were quite a number of people from Zenica, and they had nothing. They had no clothes or shoes, and they wore whatever they could lay their hands on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So in the territory or municipality of Busovaca, there were also Croat refugees from Zenica and other parts?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, were you present when a prisoner or internee complained to the International Red Cross representatives or international observers of the treatment they would receive from the guards or others in the prison? Have you ever heard anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see anyone ill-treat those people, I mean, guards or somebody else of those who were serving terms for either crimes or for disciplinary reasons?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any incidents when HVO members might try to enter the prison or did enter the prison and do something there; do you remember any such events?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When HVO soldiers would break into the prison, would the guards manage to stop those soldiers or did sometimes they manage to get in?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at times they did get in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why was it that the guards could not prevent them from entering the prison?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Because they were all armed. Everybody carried weapons, and then what? What to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know if, after such events, you or some other guard or the prison warden would notify the military command and say that steps had to be taken against such perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the warden did. He submitted a report that they had been there and that measures should be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any measures were taken against those perpetrators? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I think -- I believe there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was that a daily occurrence?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that such situations were an exception?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were an exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, you were an HVO soldier, you were a military policeman, you took part in the defence of the municipality of Busovaca, you were on the frontline. Did you ever see near you or in the municipality of Busovaca or in Kaonik a soldier bearing the insignia "HV"?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see a soldier with some other insignia other than HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, you spent almost the whole of January there, then February, March, and a large part of April, so four months you were a guard in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So during that time, you could really get familiar with the prison, with the conditions there. So could you describe to us this lower part, this lower floor where the cells were, were they locked by key or did they have a bolt or what?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: They did not have a key, but there were two bolts on the upper part of the door and on the lower part of the door. There were no keys.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many persons could be put in a cell, roughly?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, while we had those pallets (sic) there, there were perhaps five or six persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, but were there any such situations where more than five or six persons were in a cell?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was it for a long period of time or --

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was only provisional. That was that first conflict when we separated those elderly; then at times, there were even as many as 10 or 15, but they did not care that they could lie down or sit down or read, only to be warm or to be comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But that situation did not last for long?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is quite true. It did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How long did it last?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. A few days perhaps or a week, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, now I'm referring to the second conflict in particular. Do you recall any situation when the population of nearby villages, where the fighting was taking place, would they come to Kaonik seeking protection? Were there such cases?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did you do when people came to you and asked you to be shielded from the conflict? Did you let them enter and offer them shelter, or did you refuse them?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not refuse them, no. People were afraid. Skradno, for instance, it was the frontline, and those places, and they were safer there than at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you provided no (sic) accommodation and food; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But that was also for a few days or for a longer period of time?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: For several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, who were those people who asked for protection? Were they Croats, Muslims, or who?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there enough food at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe there was. For a while, we did not have three meals a day, we only had two, but it was for everybody. I mean, everybody got two meals. Simply the supply was bad, and for a while, we could not. So that for a while, we had to cut it down to two meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did it take long? How long did it last; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not -- not really. I should say for about 20, 25 days, or maybe a month, but not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But when was that? During the first or during the second conflict; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, at the time when there was enough food, did you meet the request of those persons who wanted a second helping? Could you help those who simply asked for more?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we distributed food as long as there was, and as much as we could. Yes, I know there was one who -- who was really hungry at lunchtime, and I think he had some six or seven helpings. We kept pouring him food, and he ate as long as he could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you never put any limits on the food that you had at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that you got the same food as the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: The same food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, you mentioned that there were the toilet facilities, which was a makeshift thing, and it was outside the building, outside the second hangar, but how about the first building where the cells were?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there we had the toilet facility within -- inside the prison, near the cells, so there was also a bathroom and the WC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was this the prisoners' WC?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the guards used the same facility?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they had their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So this WC was at the disposal of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, you were a prison guard for quite a long time and became familiar with conditions in the prison, at the penitentiary in Zenica. Apart from Zenica, and I'm not referring to Kaonik, did you work anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Only there. Only Zenica and Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But you do have some experience as regards the prison guards and their treatment, their attitude to prisoners; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Jerkovic, how would you describe the attitude of Mr. Aleksovski as the warden of the district military prison in Kaonik towards the prisoners and detainees, that is, the civilians also, who were brought during the first and the second conflict to Kaonik? How would you describe his attitude to them?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that Zlatko did really all he could for all these people, and I really think that these people -- that quite a number of these people should be quite grateful to Zlatko, and I mean Zlatko in person, because all that could be done through the Red Cross and through all those, all that one could -- and as far as one could, it was like that. There were no problems, visits or visits home or bringing food or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, does that mean that you did not ever hear that he ever refused to do something, to do something that was within his power?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did he ever refuse to give people food?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, come, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did he ever deny them medical help, if need be?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did he ever interfere, if such incidents occurred, did he ever report to the military police that they were happening?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did Zlatko Aleksovski, in your view -- could Zlatko Aleksovski, if you know, send a military policeman or an HVO soldier responsible for an incident punish personally or could answer disciplinary measure against him, could he do that? Did he have such authority?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But who had the authority to punish a military policeman for an omission or perhaps a transgression?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: A commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The commander of what?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, I have only just one more, a very short question. Mr. Jerkovic, you mentioned in the beginning that you organised the reception of those people and that you did what you could under the circumstances, that nobody had announced that those people would be brought in. Could you tell us, in your view, if you did what you could under the circumstances to accommodate those people in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you give them something that you -- was there something that you didn't give them and you could? I mean, were there any medicines or something that you had in storage and yet you did not provide those people with?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that all that you had at your disposal, I mean, food, doctors' help, hygiene, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, if any of those people who were temporarily in Kaonik, did he ever suffer, fall seriously?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was anyone injured, have a wound, a fracture or something?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was anybody killed within the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see anyone being beaten within Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I have just learned that measures have been taken to meet the request of Mr. Aleksovski, but it takes a long time, so that at the moment, we shall make -- and I think it is a good moment to take a break, and the break will be 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have just received another message from my client. Yesterday, a doctor visited him because his pressure has gone up, and he is asking if he could stay in the courtroom during the break because he feels much better here -- this is a larger room and the air is much better -- and not to be taken to the small room in which he was accommodated previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, I think that Mr. Aleksovski can stay here, but then we do not need 30 minutes, and in that case, the break will be 20 minutes only. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, can we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'll try it at this stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: All right. You can now continue. You can start your cross-examination, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, you said that you were working in the Zenica prison, I think, as a guard from between 1978 and 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, that prison, did that come under the administration of the Department of Justice as well?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who provided the police? Sorry, who provided the guards, I mean, the guards that were at the prison in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I think the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Niemann, I believe we have a problem. The reporter cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'll move back, Your Honours, if it's easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, you can continue, thank you very much. But perhaps you could start from the beginning because the court reporter could not hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I asked you a moment ago, and we just have to repeat it for the purposes of the court reporter, but I think it's your evidence that from 1978, or thereabouts, to 1992, you were a guard at Zenica, at the Zenica prison?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As I understand it, the prison itself came under the administration of the Department of Justice in Zenica. And the guards, they were supplied by the police, were they?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Which police do you imply, the military or the guards in the prison? Because I worked as a guard in the penitentiary which was a civilian institution, or do you imply a military institution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's really what I was trying to get at. I was wondering if you could help me with that. It was a civilian institution. Were the guards provided by the civilian police, I think you called it the MUP, or was there some other arrangement with respect to the guards?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: MUP, no, because we went to the justice ministry to be ordained in the police, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, Zenica, I take it, at least during the time you were there, was a civilian prison and not a military prison like Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: A civilian, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I think you said in 1992 you were then mobilised into the military police. You were mobilised into the military police of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that was still in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: In the Zenica penitentiary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you continued on in the Zenica prison but this time as a member of the military police of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So I take it that, at least at some time in 1992, Zenica prison changed its classification from that of a civilian prison to a military prison, because obviously you were there as a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: One of our departments -- there were five departments in the Zenica prison, and the fifth department, when we began the war with the Serbs, the number of the prisoners were decreased, they were released conditionally, so there were a small number of them. And the fifth unit was then separated. It was already separated, and then it was appointed for the Serbs who were arrested in the Zenica area, in the villages. And they were brought there in the fifth unit, and this is where I was employed, because military policemen who had no experience could not do that. So there were about four of us who were mobilised for the military police for the Bosnia-Herzegovina army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What are you saying? Are you saying that in 1992 not all the guards at the Zenica prison joined the military police of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but only some of them; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I might just get you to clarify that, if I may. Are you saying that only some of the guards joined the military police of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I need to get it clear for the transcript. That's all.

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you met Mr. Aleksovski in the Zenica prison, I think you described him as an educator. What role did he play there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he do?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: He had his own job. He was educator. He was in charge of one of the units, and he was in charge of that unit entirely. He cared about the prisoners. He was in charge of their release. He decided when they would go home or when they would be taken, about their health care, about everything. I mean, he was like a mother to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he the warden at the Zenica prison?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So somebody else was the warden, was there, at Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that was right up until the time in 1992 when you finally went to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in Zenica, was Mr. Aleksovski your superior?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But he was in a more senior position than you, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I think your evidence is that you went to Kaonik in 1993, and you arrived there before Mr. Aleksovski had taken up the position as warden or commander of the prison at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, do you know who was there ahead of him as warden or commander of the prison in Kaonik when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You didn't know who the person was that was in charge?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there anyone in charge in that stage that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was just military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So they didn't have a warden then?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
