utterances.text: Tell me about it. How did you transfer from the military police of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the HVO? How did you go about that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I sought myself the transfer because I wanted to go to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have to be discharged from the military police of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I take it you just did this off your own bat, did you? You just decided that you would join the HVO, so you left the military police of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and simply went to the HVO of your own accord?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you remember when it was, as best you can, when Mr. Aleksovski came to the Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, somewhere at the start of February, around that time, at the end of January and the beginning of February, sometime around that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You don't know whether he was there at the time the conflict started in the Busovaca region? You can't remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, just going back to the time you're in Zenica and you said the prison came under the Ministry of Justice, how did you know that? How did you know it came under the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I knew that. Simply, I knew that, because when the police was also under the justice ministry, I simply received salaries and wages from the Ministry of Justice. And we also had something for medical checkups, because the envelopes were stamped "Ministry of Justice."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went over to Kaonik, I think that's a military prison, how did you know it was a military prison? What made you believe that to be so?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I knew that because I saw that most of the people who worked there were military policemen. There were no civilians, because I wouldn't be then transferred there. I would wear another uniform. I wouldn't bear the insignia of military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you said that after about the 25th of January, 1993, because of the conflict, you couldn't get back to your home town near Zenica, so you continued staying -- or you stayed on in Kaonik. Where did you stay? Where were your accommodations in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I slept in the same room in which we worked, and the others who were from Busovaca went home. I had an office, and there was a sofa, it was near the table, and we could use it to sit on. And in the evening, I used it as a sofa bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was in the cell block, was it, part of the cell block?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Yes, in the same building, but the cells block was separate. There was a steel door, and this was before the cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is what I meant. It wasn't a cell, but it was in the same block. I think that Mr. Aleksovski's office was close to that guards' quarters as well, wasn't it, across the hall or something like that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, it was the same office. After he arrived, when he arrived there, we used it -- we worked there, and we used it to sleep as well for sometime until the office was then transferred to the lower part at the entrance, actually. At Kaonik, there's a facility where the warden use -- which the warden uses as his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. And that happened much later, I think, that the warden moved to the facility at the entrance?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. The warden, when he arrived at the facility, he used the office at the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. What about the office in the cell block, did Mr. Aleksovski use that office along with you guards as well from time to time?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, he would climb up there and he would stay in the same room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you spoke of the civilians being brought to the camp or the facility when the conflict broke out. Who determined where they were to be accommodated? I take it things were a bit cramped at the time when all these people arrived on your doorstep. Who made the decisions about where people would be accommodated?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we organised ourselves, and these were the guards who did that, because people had to be accommodated somewhere. When there was enough room, we put them in the prison building. When there was no more room, we had to use the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said that you were somewhat taken by surprise when all these people came. That's your evidence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have a meeting with Mr. Aleksovski and the other guards to determine what you were going to do with this problem that had presented itself to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. Aleksovski was not there. It was just military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, later on when Mr. Aleksovski came, did you have meetings with him about the situation there and the placement and movement of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: When he came, well, there were no people, detainees, at the upper hangar. There was nobody at the upper hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You're quite sure of that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, did you have meetings with Mr. Aleksovski from time to time as the warden meeting with the guards?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with Mr. Aleksovski because I knew him from Zenica. We stayed at a hotel in Vitez for sometime, so we had quite a good relationship, because I knew him from the Zenica prison. So when he came, we stayed together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was his procedure for communicating his orders and so forth to the guards? Would he put it on a notice board or would he have meetings or both?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, he put it on a notice board. If there was something for us, he put it on a notice board.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was this notice board located? That was in the guards' area, was it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: It was in a corridor at the entrance to the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever receive things, letters, memorandums, or did he communicate with you that way at all, that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: With me, there was no written communications. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember him sending written communications to other guards at any stage on any matter, on any sort of matter?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about drawing up the shift roster? Did Mr. Aleksovski draw up the shift roster and pin that on the notice board?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was responsible for doing that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: That was my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you would confer with him, I take it, and let him know what you decided about who would be on duty?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was a military police, he had nothing to do with that. It was our job to secure the prison. And this is in the jurisdiction of military courts, and this is what we did. And as for the other ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But Mr. Aleksovski was responsible for people certainly that would have been put there by the military court, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So if he wanted to move one of those prisoners from one place to another or, indeed, even to release him, he would have to give you an instruction about that, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If there was a need for a transfer, this is what we did. If we were told that somebody should be moved from number 5 to number 4, it was logical that we should do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I think that we have also heard evidence that the military judge who was responsible for putting people there was also concerned to see about things like hygiene, food and treatment and so forth. No doubt if there was any matters of that nature that had been passed on to Mr. Aleksovski, he would talk to you about it, would he, in your position there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, with respect to matters of medical attention and hygiene and that, some of the prisoners would speak to Mr. Aleksovski directly about those issues, would they?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think, on some occasions, he himself took civilian detainees into Busovaca for medical attention?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On other occasions, he would request some of the guards to do that or a guard to do that, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when a prisoner had sought medical attention, they would speak to the guards first or to Mr. Aleksovski, or was there no set procedure?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: We had a book in which every day, since 7.00 a.m. when we started work until breakfast, where people all had to write if they want to see a doctor. And they would be taken to see a doctor during the day. Because we had a car, we had a court, and when the car was there, when we didn't have to go to court, we would take them to go see the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Aleksovski used to drive this car?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, are you saying, is it your evidence that if guards at the prison had beaten the prisoners, that Mr. Aleksovski would take disciplinary action against them?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: There were no such cases in the prison. And as for military police, Aleksovski had nothing to do with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So Mr. Aleksovski at no stage did anything in relation to beatings of prisoners that you're aware of in terms of disciplining them or reporting them or taking action?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: There were no beatings from the military police, or if something had to be done, Mr. Aleksovski, I guess he could speak to the commander of the military police, but not to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you did mention, of course, that he reported the HVO coming into the prison. How did you know that? How do you know he reported the HVO coming into the prison and beating prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Because there were cases when he would be there and they would be there, and it is logical that they would talk about something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How do you know that he did it? How do you know that he actually took the step of reporting these HVO beating the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I know because there's a paper. I know that he reported and that measures were taken against those people, because the people who -- because there were some threats like, "Why would he report that? Why should he do that?" I mean, what do I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who threatened who?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, those who would intrude the prison in some cases. And when they threatened Mr. Aleksovski, and they were threatening him and it was a time of war, and everybody was carrying weapons, and, you know, anything could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did the guards of the prison have access to weapons?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Wouldn't they be employed against the HVO who were coming into the prison?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, taking that the prison was a building, there was no gate, for instance, like in Zenica prison, so that you can see who was coming and from where and what his intentions are. Because the arms were stacked there on the shelf, and when somebody arrives with a gun, three or four of them, what can you do? Then we have to unlock the place where the arms were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you could have locked the prison, couldn't you, if you wanted to? It wasn't locked, you said, just the bolt slipped across, but you could have locked it if you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: The door was locked. From the inside, there was a bolt, and this door was locked. And when somebody wants to get out, they would knock. So when somebody was coming at the door, we wouldn't know what was the reason, what were they wanting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But if you wanted to keep the HVO out, you could have locked the door from the inside?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So why didn't you do that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: The door, even if they were, they could simply -- they were the guards. If somebody wants to do something, there was a window where the guards were sitting, a window, just a glass, a simple glass was there, and if they wanted to do, they would just knock on the glass, and they could see you, you could see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They could have, but they didn't break in at any stage, these HVO soldiers; they'd just come in, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but who would know that they -- that we would know that they would be intruding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, I mean, if you had someone from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina come up to the camp and decide to come in, you would have stopped them from coming in at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, the interpreters are asking you to speak into the microphone. They cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Because they would have to cross the line first before coming there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The point of what I'm trying to put to you is that if you wanted to stop people from coming in, you certainly could have stopped them, and I give to you an instance that, for example, if a soldier from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina tried to gain access to the Kaonik facility, you would have stopped them?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you the following: It never happened to me, to me personally. It did happen to people who were from Busovaca, and the people who intruded in the prison were also from Busovaca, because he would come down there, in the lower part, the military police, and they knew each other from childhood, and he would simply open the door then. These people never worked in such institutions before, and they had no -- you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke of the fact that Mr. Aleksovski would allow prisoners to go -- civilians, detainees, to go home when the doctors had suggested that this was the best treatment for them. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Aleksovski -- it's your evidence that Mr. Aleksovski would also decide on whether or not they should receive special medical care as was ordered by the doctors in relation to the civilian detainees?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, if they were to receive medicines or special food or anything of that nature, Mr. Aleksovski would -- is it your evidence that he would provide for that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And Mr. Aleksovski would also decide on whether or not these civilian detainees could be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. What do you mean by "exchanged"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, you knew that prisoners were exchanged, didn't you, and that they went to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksovski was responsible for that, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Zlatko Aleksovski didn't do that on his own initiative, off his own bat. I mean, there was somebody else with whom to do the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That was the International Committee of the Red Cross representatives that you're talking about, is it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned these civilian detainees. I think you said one group came at the end of January and stayed there for some weeks. That's your evidence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, they came at the end of January, and they stayed up until when? May? April? How long did they stay there for? When were they exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it did not last more than seven or eight days, ten perhaps at the most. I don't remember the date. But ten days on the outside, a week to ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But not all of the civilian detainees were exchanged, were they? There were some that were left behind in the facility.

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe they all left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I said to you that there's been evidence before the court that not all of them left, you wouldn't disagree with that, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was your position? You were a shift commander, were you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I was a military policeman. But because I did this and I saw people did not know, then I mostly did those shifts, and I met those people, I knew people, and what could happen and what needed to be done and so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you were responsible for drawing up the roster; I think that's what you said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In order to do that, you needed to know when people would come and people would be available?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, if somebody needed to take leave or be away because of illness or anything like that, would they come to you or would they go to Mr. Aleksovski to seek permission to be absent?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: To me. To me, but there were -- but there were quite a number of such instances because some people lived somewhere, and suddenly there would be an attack of the frontline or he couldn't turn up, he could not come, and there were some people who lived right next to the frontline and it was far, and that he simply goes to the frontline and simply doesn't turn up for work because that's where his family is and where everybody is, and I go to the frontline -- I go to the frontline so that it isn't broken through, and that's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you were in the Kaonik facility working as a guard there, you would have worked on shift yourself, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't exactly work in shifts, but since I slept there, while I was there, I stayed there for a while, and afterwards ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: And afterwards, when Mr. Aleksovski came, then we worked until 2.00 or 3.00 or 5.00 and then we went to sleep in Vitez Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you and Mr. Aleksovski were actually together in the Vitez Hotel?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, at those times when you weren't at the camp, you were at the Vitez Hotel, you couldn't vouch for what was happening to the prisoners in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not really. There was a man who was the head of the shift who is responsible, who had a book, and then reported every morning -- every morning when I would come for work, he would report what has happened, if there were any new arrivals, if anybody had been released, so he had a book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If somebody had been beaten, a prisoner had been beaten during the course of the night when he was on duty, unless he reported it to you the next morning, you wouldn't know whether or not the prisoners were beaten or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Every morning, when I came to work, I would do a round of all cells, every morning, and I would talk to people, "What has been going on?" "How are you?" "Did you sleep well?" Things like that. And I think -- I believe that anyone would have complained to me if there had been any problem: This so and so has done this and that. I mean, if anything like that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I think you went to the front when the second stage of fighting broke out in April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After that, when you went to the front in April, you would have had no further connection with the Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So whatever happened after April, the conflict broke out in April, you're not able to testify about that, at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you spoke of the fact that when the civilian prisoners were brought to the camp, you took down their details on a sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you removed from them knives and things of that nature which they may have had on their possession?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, this list of prisoners was given to the warden, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, the list was submitted to Blazenka, who kept the record of all the imprisoned, detained, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was Blazenka?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. She was a military policeman too, like the rest of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was she located?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: She was located in the same room, in the same office where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: She was in charge of secretarial duties, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For the records, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And she used to work as Mr. Aleksovski's secretary?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: After a while, when we came under the Justice, yes, but while we were with the military police, worked with the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when these civilian prisoners had their names taken and their knives and so forth removed from them, you then placed them either in the cells or in the hangar, depending on the available space?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Those cells were locked from the outside, and so was the hangar, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If prisoners wanted to go to the toilet or, for some other reason, leave either the hangar or the cells, they had to draw the attention of the guards to that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And a guard would have been posted outside of the hangar and a guard would have been posted in the cellblock building as well to attend to the prisoners if they needed anything during the course of the night?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The other purpose for having the guard there was to prevent the prisoners from leaving?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were these people charged with? What was their crime?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean those --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The civilian prisoners who were brought there in February and April of 1993, what crime had they committed?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Why, there were charges filed against some of those who were with us, for murder, for -- by the court, and there were disciplinary -- there were disciplinary -- those with disciplinary transgressions who were serving a couple of days only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about them. I am talking about the civilian prisoners, the people that were rounded up by the HVO police. They were there because they were Muslim, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They hadn't committed any crime, that you knew of anyway?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, they had committed a crime, or, no, they hadn't committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not commit a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They were there awaiting their exchange, weren't they, to move into other areas such as Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They weren't there for their own protection, though, were they? They were there because they were Muslims and they had been rounded up by the HVO police.

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Primarily, they came for protection, they were there for protection, and the second reason is because the Muslims attacked us from all sides, and so you have such people right there in the town of Busovaca or surrounding villages, so we put them in this hangar for those reasons, because there was fire on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you're in Zenica prison, prior to coming to Kaonik, did you also put Serb people in Zenica for their own protection?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Those Serb people that you put in Zenica prison, were they ultimately exchanged as well, like the Muslims were?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the pallets that people slept on, they were pallets, they were packing crates, weren't they, things you use for moving heavy, I take it, ammunition around the facility?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: What were those pallets used for? I wouldn't know. I know they were made of wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They're the sort of things that forklift trucks come along and put the prongs of the forklift truck under, don't they, and lift things up?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There was a plentiful supply of these around Kaonik because it used to be an ammunition supply facility?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These pallets were put into the cells as well as into the hangar? They had pallets in the cells as well, did they not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, describe the bedding that was made available in the cells.

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: In the cells, they slept on the pallets -- no, sorry, not on the pallets, they had made cots or, rather, half of the cell was divided, and there were some boards above the floor some six -- sixty centimetres, and then there were boards and then there were straw -- I mean, what we call straw beds, but actually they were sponges, a sponge or some kind of matter. So whatever there was would be put on this board or a plank and then one blanket or perhaps two, it depended, and pallets were up there in the military hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These beds in the cells, for example, how many people were they designed to accommodate?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said it. Normally five to six individuals, under normal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So if you put 10 to 15 people in there, they'd be extensively overcrowded, at least 100 per cent overcrowded?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: People in those cells had no choice about whether or not they were located there, did they? That was a decision that either you or some other guard would make.

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, they still preferred to be there because it was warmer than up in the hangar, and that was the only choice, this or the hangar. As I've said, they liked better to stay here, even if they could only stand or sit down, because it was warmer, because there was a room, the cells were partitioned, and there were people there. It was January, snowing, it was very cold, so they preferred to be here than up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It wasn't a case of them saying, "Well, now, take me around the facility, and I'll pick the best cell for me to stay in," you just decided, didn't you? You said, "You go here" and "You go there." It wasn't up to the prisoners to decide where they were going to be located?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that there is a case ever where the prisoner decides where they will be kept and what they will do. It's not up to prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So the preference about being warmer and so forth is not something that they had much influence over in terms of where they could choose to be?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, during the first intake of civilian detainees in January, how many people in all came to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know the exact number, but I should say, I don't know, somewhere up to 200 people, 150 or 200, I wouldn't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke of the incident where the two persons were charged as a result of Muslim detainees being killed on the frontline. Do you remember mentioning that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the outcome of that case? What happened at the end of the day to those people?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean those who were charged with this? I don't know. What happened to them in the end, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when people were taken out for trench-digging, it would be either you or Mr. Aleksovski who would be responsible for determining who would go?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: He was not in charge of that, Mr. Aleksovski, but sometimes we were not there, there were only people here, for instance, the shift had -- who weren't there and we were away. Then he had a list, he had the sequence how people came, so apart from those who were sick, and he would simply read five, ten men, how many were needed, and thus they would go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He also had the authority, did he not, to decide who wouldn't go, so that if there was someone who was sick, he, Mr. Aleksovski, would say, "Well, you don't need to go trench-digging"? He did that, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did you decide from time to time which of the civilian detainees would be selected to go trench-digging, you personally decide that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why didn't you do that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Why? There was a list, I told you, and you just followed -- went down the list, except when somebody said that he was sick, "Can you leave me behind? I'm really not feeling well. Can I go tomorrow?" Well, then you just skip him and take the next one. That, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You knew he took people's names off that list, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you knew they were going to be taken out for trench-digging?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you knew that it was wrong to use civilian detainees for the purposes of digging trenches on the frontline?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know. It was a labour obligation. There were also Croats, I mean, our people, who also dug there on that same frontline. That was a labour obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So it never occurred to you that sending these civilian prisoners out to the frontline in very dangerous conditions to dig trenches might offend, for example, the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So as far as you're concerned, it was a perfectly acceptable way to behave?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did anyone ever give you a copy of the Geneva Conventions and tell you that you should study it and become familiar with its provisions?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever take it upon yourself to acquaint yourself with the provisions of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any training at any time, either when you were in the Zenica prison or in the Kaonik prison, on the provisions of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, you spoke of the fact that civilians were not refused medical care when they wanted it. But that's only as far as you know. I mean, if there were prisoners who asked for medical attention and you weren't on shift, you wouldn't know about that and couldn't comment on it, could you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I would because there was emergency cases who would be taken after my working hours; but otherwise, everything took place in the morning hours, I told you, from seven o'clock, because in the morning when I had to put down for the examination, so it was in the morning, and only exceptionally, if there were some afternoon cases, then there was usually a car on duty there. If the car was not there, then they would ask a doctor to come to the prison in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm saying that if you weren't on duty and a guard decided not to record the fact or do anything about the fact that a prisoner had sought medical attention, then you couldn't possibly know that, could you? You can't know about things when you're not there.

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally, if it was not in the book, then what? Or unless he told me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there a loudspeaker system in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you known by any nicknames or names other than the name that you've given in court, Anto Jerkovic? Do you have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What nickname are you known by?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Pancho.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know a person called Zarko Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How do you know him?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I know him from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know him during the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Niemann. Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: With all due respect to my learned friend, I think these questions go beyond the examination-in-chief, and we did not touch upon a person called Zarko Petrovic in our examination-in-chief. So in view of your decision during the former session, so that the cross-examination could not go beyond the framework, beyond the boundaries of examination-in-chief, we therefore object to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may address that? My understanding of Your Honours' rulings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me. We have not heard the end of the interpretation yet. I believe there is something that I missed. Yes, Mr. Niemann? Yes, please? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, my understanding of Your Honours' ruling related to the ambit of the indictment. It's always been the case, as I understood it, that cross-examination is at large. Otherwise, the whole exercise would be pointless. If it couldn't be at large, for example -- let me suggest to Your Honours an example. If a witness came along and told a whole series of lies, in order to demonstrate those lies, it may be necessary to embark on other areas which weren't covered in examination-in-chief in order to demonstrate that the witness is lying to the court. I'm not suggesting that's the case with this witness, but I'm saying that is the reason, the logic, behind the fact that cross-examination cannot be limited to the evidence in chief because of that and many other reasons. I can think of numerous examples. For example, a witness could be called, and counsel could specifically limit the witness to that very limited point of evidence that he wished to present to the court. But the witness could, perhaps, discuss another area of great relevance, but not something that counsel wanted to bring out of that witness. It would be absurd to say, "Well, you can't go beyond the scope of examination-in-chief in cross-examination," so as to prevent the court hearing the particular evidence that this witness was able to attest to. It also could impinge upon questions by Your Honours because, I mean, it would hardly be fair to say to the Prosecutor, "Well, you can't cross-examine about particular areas which are outside the scope of evidence in chief." Then if Your Honours wish to ask a question about something outside the evidence in chief, Your Honours could do it, but the Prosecution couldn't. So, Your Honours, it's generally regarded in those jurisdictions where cross-examination takes place. In fact, I know of no example of a jurisdiction where cross-examination occurs that it's limited strictly to evidence in chief. I know of no example of that. In fact, it's quite the contrary. In all of those jurisdictions where cross-examination is a common feature of the trial, cross-examination is generally regarded as being at regard. That doesn't mean to say that one can embark upon a cross-examination of something totally irrelevant. The admissibility of the cross-examination is always constrained by the relevance of the cross-examination, but it's never, as far as my experience is concerned, ever restricted to merely the evidence in chief, as is led by counsel who, for tactical reasons, may specifically wish to restrict the evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I think it is now time for a break. We shall decide on all this that you have just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Can you, Mr. Niemann, elaborate on the relevance of your questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I have a series of questions about persons who witnesses for the Prosecution have attested were at the camp. And I'm just exploring -- when I say "at the time camp," I'm talking of people who either were guards or HVO, that may be unclear, but they were certainly at the camp. I'm just asking the witness whether he knows of those people and in what capacity they performed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: All right. So we shall now take a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We shall resume now. The Chamber reminds you of what we have already ruled under the circumstances, that the way to Kaonik should not be too long and repetitive. We have underlined that we have Mr. Aleksovski here on trial and not anybody else. We have the indictment, and we have already said that we need to have an integral, systematic picture if we are to understand the effects which are included in the indictment in the charges against Mr. Aleksovski. Therefore, on the basis of 96(B) and (C) and 89(D), we accept that Mr. Niemann -- that the questions that Mr. Niemann was asking are admissible because they are within the boundary in the sense of these two provisions of our rules. These are, therefore, questions which do concern Mr. Aleksovski and which the Chamber needs to know if it is to have an integral and systematic picture. And this way we are not going beyond the framework of the examination-in-chief. Therefore, the Chamber decides that these questions are admissible. Mr. Niemann, you may continue. My colleague tells me that there is an error in the transcript. We have spoken of the 85(D) and 89(B). So Mr. Mikulicic, you may also ask questions on this matter. But, Mr. Niemann, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, I was just asking you before the adjournment about a person by the name Zarko Petrovic. Did you know him? I think you said that you had heard of him. Did you know of him in connection with the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I met him down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was his rank?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what his rank was, but I heard that he worked in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what his role was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about a person by the name Miro Maric; have you heard of that person?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Miro Maric, yes, there was a Miro Maric that worked with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what his rank was?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: He had no rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say, "he worked with us," he was a guard like yourself in the camp, in the facility of Kaonik, the prison?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: A military policeman, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Finally, have you heard of a person called Marko Krilic?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you know of him because of his involvement with Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He was the deputy director of the Kaonik facility, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Marko Krilic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, can you tell me what function he performed?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: A military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what rank he had?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he had no rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And Marko Krilic was similar to yourself, a guard in the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned when we were discussing the lady Blazenka that she became Mr. Aleksovski's secretary when you all came under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice. That was when Mr. Aleksovski arrived, was it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: When it fell under the jurisdiction, yes, until somebody else arrived. And then Blazenka was in charge of the books and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. So she became Mr. Aleksovski's secretary when you and her and others came under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just have a few questions in order to clarify certain answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, is the person who is named Zarko Petrovic which was mentioned by my distinguished colleague, the Prosecutor, was he employed as a guard at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was Zarko Petrovic at Kaonik in any other capacity?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, we heard here also about the release of civilians who were taken to Kaonik in two instances in February and April. Mr. Jerkovic, do you remember whether at times they were released from Kaonik, somebody from the international organisations was present like the Red Cross and similar organisations?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Jerkovic, whether these persons, when they were released from Kaonik, when they were asked in front of these international representatives, where did they want to go?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Jerkovic, again, do you know whether some of the persons who were released, to a greater or a lesser extent, were going back to their homes, Busovaca and the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I know that most of them, the majority, I think that most of them went to Zenica. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: There are no further questions for the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO NAVIA
utterances.text: I have only one question. Do you know the name of the commander of the military unit used to take the prisoners to trench digging?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO NAVIA
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Jerkovic, I should also like to ask you a few questions. If I understood you properly, you said that someone asked that a number of persons be taken to dig trenches; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Who was it who asked for a number of these persons?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they would come from the frontline. They would go to the commander and they would say how many men they needed and we would give them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But did you know which was their rank or the organisation or the person or anything?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they would come -- they would come by car, and there would be a couple of them from the HVO army, and they would take five or ten men, as many as they needed for digging, and they would go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So those were HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And another question: You also said that there was a list of persons who dug trenches. Who compiled those lists?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a list of all people who came here, and we went down that list, except that we excluded people of advanced age and those who were sick or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, but who compiled the list? Do you know who made the list? Was it you who made that list?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody made those lists. I was there, and if they told me they needed five men or ten men, so I would read them out if I was there or the shift leader or whoever there was would read them out, and then give as many as were needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Finally, let me go back. Did you get that list? But did you know who made those lists, who compiled those lists? Who decided what names would be put on the list?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when people came, when they came, I would take down their names. I would search them to take off -- to remove the list of things. That list was with me on the desk, on Blazenka's desk. And when they would come, we would take out this list and say, "Well, we've come down to here," and you call them out. And if this one was sick or something, then you skip him and take the next one. And if they come the next day, then we would do the same thing. And we would reach the number, I don't know, 10 or 15, and then we would proceed down the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me for insisting on this matter, but those were HVO soldiers? Were they guards or you or Mr. Aleksovski who made the list?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying it again. I would take this list and take them -- those men, I would make a list of ten men, for instance. A person would make a list of ten men, and we would -- some of those people and send them to work. And the next day, it would be the shift leader, whoever happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We already know that you have answered a question from the Prosecution regarding your education, your knowledge, your familiarity with the Geneva Conventions. But have you received any instruction? Have you been instructed? Have you gone through any training for a guard?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Where did you receive the training?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: It was under the Ministry of Justice or outside it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO JERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was under the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Right. We have no further questions, Mr. Jerkovic, to ask you. Thank you for coming here and we wish you a pleasant return home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence would like to call there next witness. It is Mr. Darko Kristo. But since it is already 1.00 p.m., the Defence will probably not be able to finish the questioning until the end of the working hours of the Court, so we will continue tomorrow, or perhaps it would be better not to start even today and continue tomorrow with the questioning of this witness. It's up to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, what do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It's a matter for Your Honours. Our position on this is whatever is most convenient to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I believe it is still very important not to make breaks, not to make unnecessary interruptions. Perhaps it would be better to begin tomorrow and then make the best use of the time tomorrow, so that we shall resume tomorrow with your next witness. So until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 12.49 p.m. to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 30th day of June, 1998 at 9.00 a.m.
